strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: the lack of instance-level descriptive captions in organismal biology, which limits natural-language supervision for biological foundation models.

Proposes a practical domain-specific caption generation pipeline that combines Wikipedia-derived visual information and taxon-tailored format examples to reduce MLLM hallucination and produce faithful, instance-specific captions.

Introduces BioCAP, a CLIP-style model trained with both species labels and synthetic captions, and uses separate visual projectors for heterogeneous supervision; the design is well-motivated and validated by ablation.

Provides extensive empirical evaluation: zero-shot species classification across 10 benchmarks and natural-language retrieval tasks, with BioCAP outperforming BioCLIP and other baselines by substantial margins (e.g., +8.8% classification, +21.3% language tasks on average).
Includes informative ablation studies on caption generation strategies, dual-projector design, training set components, and the effect of Wikipedia coverage, supporting the main claims.
Conducts human evaluation of generated captions across groundedness, specificity, completeness, and clarity, showing that the full pipeline is strongly preferred over simpler prompting strategies.
Offers rich qualitative analysis using Grad-CAM, Finer-CAM, and t-SNE to demonstrate that captions help the model focus on diagnostic traits and biological semantics.
Reproducibility is strong: code, dataset, prompts, hyperparameters, and benchmark details are released or clearly specified.
Ethical considerations and limitations are discussed, including the intended research use of generated captions and the lack of IRB requirement for the human study.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: synthetic captions for CLIP-style training are already well-explored (e.g., LaCLIP, VeCLIP, CapsFusion), and the main novelty here is domain-specific context engineering rather than a fundamentally new method.

Evaluation is limited to a ViT-B/16 CLIP backbone and zero-shot classification/retrieval; there is no fine-tuning, no broader multimodal evaluation (e.g., VQA, detection), and no comparison with more recent or larger biological foundation models such as BioCLIP 2.

The retrieval benchmarks (Cornell Bird, PlantID) are newly collected by the authors; while details are provided, they are not standard community benchmarks, and potential overlap or leakage with training data is not fully analyzed.

Human evaluation relies mostly on computer science students (15/16 participants) with only one ecologist, which limits domain expertise for judging fine-grained biological fidelity; inter-rater agreement is only moderate (Gwet's AC1 ≈ 0.615).
The theoretical analysis in Appendix A uses a simplified linear model and does not rigorously establish the claimed causal benefits of captions; it is illustrative rather than a formal guarantee.

Caption generation depends on a single MLLM (InternVL3 38B) and Wikipedia coverage is only 29.5% of taxa; the impact of MLLM choice, extraction errors, and coverage limitations is not thoroughly explored.

Captions include the species name, which could confound the benefit of trait supervision; although ablations suggest traits matter, the separation between label and caption supervision is not fully isolated.

Some benchmark gains are extremely large (e.g., PlantID retrieval), which may warrant additional analysis of benchmark difficulty, distribution shift, or potential data artifacts to fully convince a skeptical reviewer.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: the lack of instance-level descriptive captions for organismal biology images, which limits natural-language supervision in biological foundation models.

Proposes a sensible domain-specific caption generation pipeline that uses Wikipedia-derived visual information and taxon-tailored format examples to reduce MLLM hallucination and produce more faithful, trait-focused captions.
Reports consistent improvements over BioCLIP and other baselines across ten zero-shot species classification benchmarks, with an average absolute gain of 8.8 percentage points.
Includes thorough ablation studies that isolate the effects of caption type, prompt design, domain-specific contexts, and the dual-projector architecture.
Provides human evaluation of caption quality and qualitative analyses (Grad-CAM, t-SNE) that help explain why caption supervision improves classification and semantic alignment.
The paper is generally well-written and well-structured, with extensive appendix material documenting prompts, hyperparameters, and benchmark details.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: training CLIP-style models with synthetic captions is already well-established (e.g., LaCLIP, VeCLIP, CapsFusion). The contribution here is primarily domain-specific engineering and application rather than a fundamentally new method.

Missing comparison to existing caption-augmentation methods on the same biological data. The internal ablation compares Base/Trait/Example+Wiki, but it does not show whether the proposed pipeline outperforms generic caption augmentation or caption rewriting approaches.

The two newly collected retrieval benchmarks (Cornell Bird, PlantID) are not standard, and their construction is not fully specified. It is unclear whether text-image pairs contain species names, how species overlap with TreeOfLife-10M is handled, and whether the texts are instance-specific. The large gains on these benchmarks drive the headline 21.3% average improvement, making that result less robust.

No statistical significance, confidence intervals, or multiple training runs are reported. All main results appear to come from single runs, which is a concern given the large number of benchmarks and the scale of training.

The human evaluation relies mostly on non-expert evaluators (15 computer science students and only one ecologist), which may not reliably assess biological groundedness, specificity, and scientific accuracy of captions.

The theoretical analysis in Appendix A is overly simplistic: it assumes linear transformations and shared noise between image and caption, and does not rigorously justify the causal claims about captions improving trait alignment.
Claims about improved behavior understanding are supported only by qualitative t-SNE and Grad-CAM visualizations, without quantitative evaluation on behavior recognition or related tasks.

The main comparison to BioCLIP would be stronger if a label-only baseline were trained with the exact same recipe, data, and 50-epoch schedule on TreeOfLife-10M. Relying on prior BioCLIP numbers may confound the effect of captions with differences in training details.
Reproducibility is partially limited by missing URLs/links in the manuscript (apparently redacted) and by insufficient detail on caption quality for species not covered by Wikipedia.

strengths: Addresses an underexplored and practically important problem: providing natural-language supervision for organismal biology, where instance-level captions are scarce and most data have only taxonomic labels.

Proposes a sensible and effective domain-specific caption generation pipeline that uses Wikipedia-derived visual information and taxon-tailored format examples to reduce MLLM hallucination and produce faithful, instance-specific captions.

Introduces BioCAP with separate visual projectors for taxonomic labels and captions, yielding substantial and consistent gains over BioCLIP and other baselines: +8.8% average on 10 zero-shot species classification benchmarks and +21.3% average on natural-language/retrieval tasks.

Provides comprehensive ablations on caption strategy, domain-specific context components, projector design, training epochs, and Wikipedia-covered vs. non-covered species, showing that the proposed captions generalize beyond species with Wikipedia coverage.

Includes human evaluation of caption quality with inter-rater agreement statistics, plus qualitative analyses (Grad-CAM, t-SNE) that support the claim that captions encourage attention to diagnostic biological traits and broader semantics.
Reproducibility is strong: code and data are released, and the appendix provides prompts, hyperparameters, benchmark details, and implementation specifics.
The paper is clearly written and well organized, with informative figures and tables that make the contribution and empirical results easy to follow.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is moderate: synthetic captioning for CLIP-style training is well established, and the main novelty is the domain-specific context injection (Wikipedia visual information and taxon-tailored format examples) for biology. This may be viewed as a strong domain adaptation/application rather than a fundamentally new multimodal learning method.

Caption generation depends on Wikipedia coverage, which is only 29.5% of taxa and 52.3% of samples at the species level. Although the ablation suggests generalization to non-covered species, the quality and failure modes of captions for uncovered taxa could be analyzed further.

The human evaluation relies on a relatively small pool of annotators (16 participants, mostly CS students with only one ecologist) and 200 images. Expert biological validation would strengthen the claims about caption faithfulness and specificity.

The retrieval benchmarks (PlantID and Cornell Bird) are newly collected. The paper does not explicitly discuss decontamination or overlap with TreeOfLife-10M training data, which could affect the reported retrieval gains if any images or near-duplicates appear in training.
The theoretical justification in Appendix A is a simplified linear model and provides intuition rather than a rigorous analysis of why captions improve nonlinear contrastive representation learning.

BioCAP does not achieve the best performance on all natural-language tasks: on INQUIRE-Rerank Behavior and Context, it is below CLIP and SigLIP, indicating that the additional caption supervision does not uniformly improve every semantic dimension.

strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored problem: the lack of instance-level textual descriptions in organismal biology for multimodal foundation models, and demonstrates the value of descriptive captions beyond taxonomic labels.

Proposes a well-motivated caption generation pipeline that incorporates domain knowledge from Wikipedia-derived visual information and taxon-tailored format examples to reduce hallucination and produce faithful, instance-specific captions.
Introduces BioCAP with a dual-projector design to handle heterogeneous supervision (taxonomic labels and captions), effectively leveraging both signals while sharing the visual and text encoders.

Conducts extensive and convincing evaluation: zero-shot species classification on 10 benchmarks, text-image retrieval on 2 benchmarks, INQUIRE-Rerank, few-shot classification, additional biological visual tasks, and detailed ablations.

Achieves strong empirical results: consistent improvements over BioCLIP, CLIP, SigLIP, FG-CLIP, and BioTrove-CLIP across classification and retrieval, with an average classification gain of 8.8% and substantial retrieval gains.

Provides thorough ablation studies: caption strategies (Base, Trait, Trait+Example, Trait+Example+Wiki), number of format examples, MLLM family and size, training set components, dual vs. single projector, and training epoch fairness.

Includes qualitative and quantitative analyses (Grad-CAM, Finer-CAM, t-SNE, energy-based pointing game) that support the claim that captions guide the model to focus on diagnostic traits and biological semantics.
Human evaluation of caption quality shows clear preference for the proposed pipeline, with reported inter-evaluator agreement.
Good reproducibility: code and dataset are claimed to be released, and the appendix provides detailed hyperparameters, prompts, and experimental settings.
Clear writing, well-structured presentation, and an ethical statement that acknowledges potential risks and limits of generated captions.
weaknesses: The core idea of using synthetic captions for CLIP-style training is not entirely new; the main novelty lies in domain-specific context injection and application to biological foundation models, which may be seen as incremental by some reviewers.

The two custom retrieval benchmarks (PlantID and Cornell Bird) are collected by the authors and may be biased toward the descriptive caption style generated by MLLMs; although INQUIRE-Rerank provides a standard benchmark, the very large gains on custom benchmarks warrant cautious interpretation.

Few-shot classification and some additional biological visual tasks show limited or inconsistent improvements over BioCLIP (e.g., Table 18 and Table 19), indicating that the benefits are mainly for zero-shot and descriptive retrieval rather than broad visual representation learning.

The human evaluation relies heavily on computer science students (15 of 16 participants), with only one domain expert (ecologist), which may limit the reliability of judgments on biological trait specificity and completeness.
No statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are reported for the main results, making it difficult to assess whether some smaller improvements are meaningful.
The theoretical analysis in Appendix A is a simplified linear model that does not fully capture the complexity of MLLM-generated captions, noise structures, and contrastive learning dynamics.
The reproducibility statement in the provided manuscript contains missing links (e.g., 'at .'), leaving the actual code and dataset locations unclear.

Some manual curation steps (e.g., validating format examples via Gemini Deep Research and human review) may limit scalability and introduce subjectivity, even though stability across generation rounds is demonstrated.

strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored problem: the lack of instance-level natural language supervision in organismal biology, where most data are annotated only with species names.

Proposes a domain-specific synthetic caption generation pipeline that incorporates Wikipedia-derived visual information and taxon-tailored format examples to reduce hallucination and improve instance specificity.

Provides a comprehensive empirical suite: zero-shot classification on 10 benchmarks, retrieval on INQUIRE-Rerank plus two collected benchmarks, and ablations on caption strategy, projector design, training set components, MLLM choice, and example count.
Reports consistent improvements over BioCLIP and other baselines on zero-shot species classification and text-image retrieval.
Includes qualitative analyses (Grad-CAM, t-SNE) and a human evaluation with inter-annotator agreement statistics to support caption quality claims.
Provides substantial reproducibility details, including prompts, hyperparameters, data statistics, and a statement that code/data will be released.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: synthetic captioning for CLIP-style training is well established (e.g., LaCLIP, VeCLIP, CapsFusion, FG-CLIP). The contribution is an incremental application of these ideas to biology with domain-specific context engineering, and it does not compare against strong general-domain captioning baselines adapted to this setting.

Potential confound in the central comparison: BioCAP is trained for 50 epochs with a global batch size of 32768, while the BioCLIP baseline numbers appear to be taken from prior work with different training recipes. The paper does not state that BioCLIP was retrained under identical settings, so the reported 8.8% average improvement may partly reflect training-recipe differences rather than captions alone.

Lack of statistical rigor: main results have no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests, and most experiments appear to be single-run. Claims of 8.8% and 21.3% improvements are therefore not statistically supported, especially on smaller benchmarks.

The theoretical analysis in Appendix A is a simplistic linear model that assumes shared latent traits and independent noise. It does not rigorously justify the method, make testable predictions, or connect convincingly to the actual contrastive training dynamics.

Few-shot classification and additional biological visual tasks show little to no improvement, and sometimes BioCAP is worse than BioCLIP. This undermines broad claims about learning rich biological semantics or general multimodal understanding.

Human evaluation is limited: participants are mostly computer science students with only one ecologist, evaluation is not clearly blind to method identity, and longer, more detailed captions from the proposed method may bias preference. Inter-annotator agreement is only moderate.

The new retrieval benchmarks are non-standard, and the extremely large gains (e.g., PlantID I2T 82.6 vs 48.4 for BioCLIP) are surprising. Despite duplicate control, distribution overlap or stylistic matching between synthetic training captions and benchmark texts is not fully ruled out.

The 'beyond labels' framing is misleading: captions are generated using species labels, Wikipedia visual descriptions, and taxon-tailored examples, and they include the species name. The additional supervision is therefore largely label-derived rather than independent of labels.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the reproducibility statement contains missing URLs, and the pipeline relies on proprietary Gemini Deep Research plus manual curation of format examples, which may be difficult for others to replicate exactly.

strengths: Addresses a clear and important gap: organismal biology lacks instance-level descriptive captions, and the paper shows how synthetic captions can provide complementary supervision beyond taxonomic labels.

Proposes a practical and scalable caption-generation pipeline that injects domain knowledge via Wikipedia-derived visual information and taxon-tailored format examples, effectively reducing MLLM hallucination and yielding faithful, instance-specific captions.

Demonstrates strong empirical gains: BioCAP consistently outperforms BioCLIP and CLIP across ten zero-shot species classification benchmarks (average +8.8% over BioCLIP) and on biological text-image retrieval benchmarks (average +21.9% over BioCLIP in Table 2).

Provides a thorough evaluation suite, including ablations on caption strategy, dual projectors, training-set components, format-example count, MLLM family and model size, as well as human evaluation of caption quality and qualitative Grad-CAM/t-SNE analyses.
Strong reproducibility and transparency: code and dataset are released, prompts and hyperparameters are detailed, computational costs are reported, and ethical/licensing considerations are discussed.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: synthetic captioning for CLIP-style training is well established in the general domain, and the core contribution is the domain-specific context injection and application to biological foundation models rather than a fundamentally new learning paradigm.

Main zero-shot classification and retrieval results are reported without variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, which makes it harder to assess the robustness of the reported gains.

Some comparisons are not fully controlled: FG-CLIP, SigLIP, and BioTrove-CLIP are trained with different data/compute budgets, so only BioCLIP is a directly comparable baseline; the newly collected retrieval benchmarks are relatively small and may not fully establish external validity.
Few-shot classification results are mixed, with BioCAP not consistently outperforming BioCLIP or other baselines on some benchmarks (e.g., NABirds), somewhat limiting the claimed breadth of benefits.

Human evaluation of caption quality is useful but limited in scale and expertise: 200 images and mostly non-expert evaluators, with only moderate inter-evaluator agreement on groundedness/specificity; additional expert annotation would strengthen the claim.
The theoretical analysis in Section A is simplistic and not central to the empirical contribution; there are also minor reporting inconsistencies (e.g., 21.3% vs. 21.9% improvements) and table typos.
